idiom_name: final null subclass + function-local static instance + default reference parameter
implementation_notes: The classic structure is the language idiom here: an abstract interface with virtual functions, a final null subclass overriding every one of them with an empty body, and one shared instance returned by a static accessor (Logger::null()), so a reference-typed parameter defaults to the null collaborator and callers never hold a nullable pointer. Mark the null class final so the compiler can devirtualise when the concrete type is visible, and keep the instance in a function-local static - C++11 guarantees that its initialisation is thread-safe. Choose the policy-template variant instead when the null/real decision is fixed at compile time and the call is hot; choose std::optional instead when absence must stay visible to the caller.
pitfalls: Returning a raw pointer keeps nullptr semantically possible and keeps the guards alive; hand out a reference (or a non-null wrapper) so the call sites cannot be null.

A null subclass that inherits from the concrete real class silently gains real behaviour for every virtual function added later; implement the interface, or keep the null class next to the interface so a new method breaks the build.
Function-local statics are thread-safe to initialise, but destruction order at exit is unspecified - do not let the null instance depend on other globals.

variants.name: Compile-time null policy (template parameter)
variants.idiom_name: empty policy struct as a defaulted template parameter
variants.implementation_notes: When the null-or-real decision is fixed per instantiation, pass the behaviour as a template parameter and give it an empty policy type as the default: template <class LogPolicy = NoLog>. The compiler then eliminates the no-op calls entirely and can inline the real path aggressively, which is why this form wins on hot paths where dispatch to a runtime null object would still cost an indirect call per event. The cost is a distinct instantiation per policy (object-code growth) and the loss of runtime swapping; keep the runtime form whenever the collaborator is injected after construction.
pitfalls: Every policy combination is a separate instantiation, so a growing policy set multiplies object code; use it for the one hot collaborator, not for every dependency.
A policy cannot be injected, replaced or spied on at run time; if tests must swap the null policy after construction, the runtime variant is the right form.
